books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 A: More than four million Americans crossed the Appalachian Mountains between 1800 and 1840 to settle in the West. Many Southern planters moved into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, and later Texas, hoping to recreate the Cotton Kingdom, complete with slave labor, on cheaper land. Farmers from the upper South moved into southern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, while New England and New York families settled in northern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, as well as Wisconsin and Michigan. Over time, the towns and churches of the Old Northwest began to resemble New England, while the plantations of the newly settled South resembled the Old South. Meanwhile, most immigrants who arrived between 1800 and 1860 came from northern and western Europe. Four-fifths of Irish immigrants settled in port cities of the Northeast, while German immigrants, often with more money, moved on to the “German triangle” of Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Milwaukee.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 A. Paraphrased, not quoted.

stem: According to the passage, Irish and German settlement patterns differed in that

options.text: Irish immigrants settled mainly in Northeast port cities, while German immigrants moved on to Midwestern cities
German immigrants settled mainly in Southern port cities, while Irish immigrants farmed the Great Plains
options.misconception: The books place the Irish in Northeast cities and the Germans in the Midwestern German triangle, the other way around.

options.text: both groups settled mainly in the rural South as plantation workers
options.misconception: Neither group settled the plantation South; the Irish stayed in Northern cities and the Germans went west to cities like Cincinnati and Milwaukee.

options.text: both groups returned to Europe after a few years
options.misconception: Most stayed; the Irish crowded into port cities and the Germans built lasting Midwestern communities.

rationales.A: Four-fifths of Irish immigrants settled in Northeast port cities like New York and Boston. German immigrants, often with more money, moved on to Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Milwaukee, the German triangle.
rationales.B: The pattern runs the other way. The Irish stayed in the Northeast; the Germans moved west to the Midwestern triangle.
rationales.C: Neither group worked the plantations. The Irish took city and canal work in the North, and the Germans settled Midwestern cities and farms.
rationales.D: Return migration was small. Both groups stayed and built communities that lasted.
rationales.general:
1. Place the Irish. Four-fifths settled in Northeast port cities like New York and Boston.
2. Place the Germans. They moved on to Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Milwaukee, the German triangle.
3. Ask why the paths split. The Germans often had more money to travel beyond the port; the Irish usually did not.
Background: The Irish were the largest immigrant group of the period, driven out by famine, while Germans were the second largest and often arrived with skills and savings.
Remember: two groups can cross the same ocean and settle in different Americas.
